---
title: "Outline and Writing Requirements"
---

This document is the master plan for the book. It is intentionally committed **before**
the chapters so the structure and the acceptance criteria for every section can be
audited and amended cheaply. Each chapter is then written by a dedicated writer
against the requirements stated here, and later verified for citation accuracy.

## Scope and audience

**Subject.** How biological entities — DNA/RNA sequences, proteins, protein
structures, small molecules, cells, and biological networks — are turned into
vector representations ("embeddings"), and how those representations are used,
evaluated, and interpreted.

**Reader.** Computational biologists, bioinformaticians, and ML practitioners who
know some biology and some machine learning and want a single, coherent, citation-
backed treatment that connects the two.

**Non-goals.** This is not a textbook on deep learning theory, nor a tools manual.
Where a method matters we state *what it does, why it works, when it fails*, and
cite the primary source instead of re-deriving it.

## Conventions (apply to every chapter)

- Language: English, present tense, third person, no marketing tone.
- Every factual claim about a named method gets a citation to the **primary
  source** (the original paper), not a blog post or a review, unless a review is
  explicitly the subject.
- Definitions box for each central term: a `::: {.callout-note}` titled
  "Definition".
- Every chapter ends with a **Key Takeaways** callout (3–6 bullets) and a
  **Further Reading** list (3–6 entries with links/DOIs).
- Use `[@key]` Pandoc citation syntax; every key MUST exist in `references.bib`.
  Never invent a BibTeX entry. If the citation cannot be verified, omit it and
  write the claim without an attribution.
- Math in `$...$`/`$$...$$` (MathJax). Keep notation consistent with Appendix A.
- Code blocks are illustrative and short (≤ ~20 lines), language-tagged, and
  must be runnable in principle.
- Target length per chapter: **2,000–3,500 words** of body text.

## Acceptance criteria ("definition of done") for a chapter

1. All required subsections are present and in order.
2. Every named method/model is cited to its primary source in `references.bib`.
3. At least one figure or table per major subsection group (may be a described
   diagram, a comparison table, or a rendered figure).
4. `quarto render` succeeds with **no broken citation keys** and no undefined
   cross-references.
5. Key Takeaways + Further Reading present.
6. No fabricated numbers; any quantitative claim is either cited or explicitly
   labelled as illustrative.

# Part I — Foundations

## Chapter 1 — Why Embeddings for Biology?
*File:* `chapters/01-why-embeddings.qmd`

**Purpose.** Motivate representation learning for biological data and set up the
vocabulary used throughout the book.

**Required sections**
1. The representation problem in biology (heterogeneous, high-dimensional,
   noisy, structured data).
2. From hand-crafted features to learned representations (one-hot, k-mers,
   physicochemical descriptors → learned vectors).
3. What makes biology different: sequence vs. structure, sparsity, batch
   effects, evolutionary signal, small labeled datasets.
4. Types of embeddings (feature, contextual, structural, joint/multimodal) and
   a unifying notation table.
5. A map of the book (how Parts I–III fit together).

**Required artifacts.** One table classifying embedding types by input modality;
one "taxonomy of biological data" figure (described or drawn).

**Key citations.** Bengio et al. representation learning; Mikolov word2vec;
Alley et al. Unified Rational Protein Features; Jumper et al. AlphaFold (as a
motivating structural example).

**Done when.** A reader who stops here can state why learned embeddings are
useful and can name the modalities covered later.

## Chapter 2 — Mathematical Foundations of Representation Learning
*File:* `chapters/02-math-foundations.qmd`

**Purpose.** Give the minimum mathematical toolkit: vectors, similarity,
distances, manifolds, and dimensionality reduction.

**Required sections**
1. Vectors, norms, dot products, cosine similarity, and when each is appropriate.
2. Distance metrics for biological data (Euclidean, cosine, Mahalanobis,
   edit/alignment distances as non-Euclidean examples).
3. Curse of dimensionality and the manifold hypothesis in biology.
4. Dimensionality reduction: PCA, t-SNE, UMAP — what each preserves and the
   common misinterpretations.
5. Embedding spaces: linear structure, anisotropy, alignment (Procrustes,
   orthogonal Procrustes), and analogy operations.

**Required artifacts.** A metric cheat-sheet table; a figure (described)
contrasting what PCA/t-SNE/UMAP preserve.

**Key citations.** Pearson PCA; van der Maaten & Hinton t-SNE; McInnes et al.
UMAP; Smith et al. (UMAP pitfalls); Mikolov analogy arithmetic.

**Done when.** Notation matches Appendix A and every metric is defined formally.

## Chapter 3 — Learning Embeddings: from PCA to Deep Networks
*File:* `chapters/03-learning-embeddings.qmd`

**Purpose.** Explain how embeddings are *learned*: objectives and architectures.

**Required sections**
1. Matrix factorization and spectral methods (PCA/SVD, LSA, spectral embedding).
2. Shallow prediction methods (word2vec SGNS/CBOW, GloVe, node2vec).
3. Autoencoders and VAEs (reconstruction, variational objective, latent space).
4. Contrastive and metric learning (InfoNCE, triplet loss, SimCLR) and why it
   dominates biological foundation models.
5. Self-supervised pretraining then fine-tuning vs. linear probing.
6. Masked-language-modeling in the biological sequence setting.

**Required artifacts.** Objective-function table (method → loss → what it
optimizes); a figure showing the pretrain→probe/finetune pipeline.

**Key citations.** Mikolov word2vec; Pennington GloVe; Kingma & Welling VAE;
van den Oord CPC/InfoNCE; Chen et al. SimCLR; Devlin BERT; Hamilton GraphSAGE.

**Done when.** Each objective is stated as an equation with its variables defined.

# Part II — Biological Modalities

## Chapter 4 — DNA and RNA Sequence Embeddings
*File:* `chapters/04-dna-rna.qmd`

**Purpose.** Cover representations of nucleotide sequences.

**Required sections**
1. Classical encodings: one-hot, k-mer counts, k-mer hashing, mismatch kernels.
2. Unsupervised sequence vectors: dna2vec / k-mer embeddings.
3. Supervised CNNs and the regulatory-genome era (DeepSEA, Basset).
4. Transformer language models: DNABERT, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer,
   HyenaDNA, Evo.
5. RNA-specific embeddings: RNA-FM and structure-aware models.
6. Practicalities: sequence length limits, tokenization schemes (k-mer vs. BPE
   vs. single nucleotide), reverse-complement equivariance.

**Required artifacts.** Model comparison table (model, tokenizer, max length,
pretraining corpus, params); a diagram of k-mer tokenization vs. BPE.

**Key citations.** Alipanahi DeepSEA; Kelley Basset; Ji DNABERT; Zhou DNABERT-2;
Dalla-Torre Nucleotide Transformer; Nguyen HyenaDNA; Chen RNA-FM.

**Done when.** The tokenization/context-length trade-offs are explicit.

## Chapter 5 — Protein Sequence Embeddings
*File:* `chapters/05-proteins-sequence.qmd`

**Purpose.** Representations of amino-acid sequences, the crown jewel of
biological embeddings.

**Required sections**
1. Classical features: k-mer/PSSM, HMM profiles, physicochemical scales.
2. Unsupervised protein vectors: ProtVec, UniRep.
3. Supervised/transfer baselines: TAPE benchmarks.
4. Protein language models: ProtBERT/ProtBERT-BFD, ESM-1b, ESM-2, ESMFold
   (embedding angle), ProtT5, Ankh.
5. What the representations encode: structure, function, mutational effects;
   probing studies.
6. Practicalities: MSAs vs. single-sequence models, scaling laws, compute.

**Required artifacts.** PLM comparison table; a figure of the embedding →
downstream-task transfer pipeline.

**Key citations.** Asgari ProtVec; Alley UniRep; Rao TAPE; Elnaggar ProtTrans/
ProtBERT/ProtT5; Rives ESM-1b; Lin ESM-2; Ahdritz OpenFold; Elnaggar Ankh;
Brandes et al. (what PLMs learn).

**Done when.** The MSA-based vs. single-sequence distinction is clear and cited.

## Chapter 6 — Protein Structure Embeddings
*File:* `chapters/06-protein-structure.qmd`

**Purpose.** Embeddings of 3D structure and structure-aware representations.

**Required sections**
1. Representing structure: coordinates, distance matrices, contact maps, graphs.
2. Invariance/equivariance: rotation, translation, permutation.
3. GNN and geometric methods: GVP-GNN, EGNN, GearNet, ProteinMPNN.
4. Structure as a teacher: AlphaFold/ESMFold representations and their use as
   features; inverse folding (ESM-IF).
5. Fold embeddings: TM-vector and structural-alphabet approaches.
6. Linking sequence and structure embeddings.

**Required artifacts.** Equivariance/invariance table; a figure contrasting
coordinate vs. graph representations.

**Key citations.** Jing GVP-GNN; Satorras EGNN; Zhang GearNet; Dauparas
ProteinMPNN; Hsu TM-vec; Hsu ESM-IF; Jumper AlphaFold2; Zhang et al. structure
vs. sequence representations.

**Done when.** The invariance requirements of each architecture are stated.

## Chapter 7 — Molecular and Chemical Embeddings
*File:* `chapters/07-molecules-chemistry.qmd`

**Purpose.** Representations of small molecules.

**Required sections**
1. Classical fingerprints (ECFP/Morgan, MACCS) and physicochemical descriptors.
2. String-based learned embeddings: SMILES, Mol2Vec, ChemBERTa, MolBERT.
3. Graph neural networks for molecules (MPNN, D-MPNN, GIN, AttentiveFP).
4. Pretraining strategies for molecular LMs (masked atom modeling).
5. Conformers and 3D-aware models (GemNet, Uni-Mol).
6. Property/activity prediction and the role of embeddings.

**Required artifacts.** Fingerprint vs. learned-embedding comparison table;
molecule→graph→embedding figure.

**Key citations.** Rogers & Hahn ECFP; Jaeger Mol2Vec; Chithrananda ChemBERTa;
Gilmer MPNN; Yang Chemprop D-MPNN; Yang Uni-Mol; Zhou Uni-Mol (3D).

**Done when.** The reader can choose between fingerprints and learned embeddings
for a given QSAR/QSPR task.

## Chapter 8 — Single-Cell Embeddings
*File:* `chapters/08-single-cell.qmd`

**Purpose.** Embeddings of cells and genes from single-cell omics.

**Required sections**
1. The data: count matrices, sparsity, dropout, library size.
2. Classical pipelines: normalization, HVG selection, PCA, neighborhood graphs,
   UMAP/t-SNE visualization.
3. Probabilistic latent models: scVI, scANVI, totalVI, and batch correction.
4. Cell foundation models: scBERT, Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation.
5. Gene embeddings and transfer learning across datasets.
6. Evaluation: integration metrics (kBET, LISI), and why UMAP is not a
   quantitative benchmark.

**Required artifacts.** Integration-metrics table; a diagram of the standard
scRNA-seq latent-variable pipeline.

**Key citations.** Lopez scVI; Wolf Scanpy; Luecken benchmarking; Yang scBERT;
Theodoris Geneformer; Cui scGPT; Hao Seurat; Luecken/LISI/kBET.

**Done when.** Batch-effect handling and evaluation caveats are explicit.

## Chapter 9 — Multi-Omics and Multimodal Integration
*File:* `chapters/09-multiomics-multimodal.qmd`

**Purpose.** Joint embeddings across modalities.

**Required sections**
1. The integration problem: shared vs. modality-specific factors.
2. Early/intermediate/late fusion and shared-latent-space models (MOFA,
   MultiVI, Cobolt).
3. Contrastive multimodal alignment: CLIP-style objectives in biology
   (sequence–structure, image–omics).
4. Translation between modalities (e.g., image→expression, sequence→structure).
5. Missing modalities and partial observability.
6. Case study: spatial transcriptomics embeddings.

**Required artifacts.** Fusion-strategy comparison table; a shared-latent-space
figure.

**Key citations.** Argelaguet MOFA+; Gayoso MultiVI; Gong Cobolt; Radford CLIP;
Ashuach MultiVI; spatial methods (Tangram, SpaGCN).

**Done when.** The trade-off between alignment and modality-specific
information is quantified conceptually.

## Chapter 10 — Graphs, Networks, and Knowledge-Graph Embeddings
*File:* `chapters/10-graphs-knowledge.qmd`

**Purpose.** Embeddings of relational biological data.

**Required sections**
1. Biological graphs: PPI, regulatory, metabolic, gene–disease.
2. Shallow node embeddings: DeepWalk, node2vec, LINE.
3. Graph neural networks: GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, message passing.
4. Knowledge-graph embeddings: TransE, RotatE, ComplEx and link prediction.
5. Applications: drug repurposing, target identification, function prediction.
6. Heterogeneity and scale.

**Required artifacts.** GNN layer variants table; a KG link-prediction figure.

**Key citations.** Perozzi DeepWalk; Grover node2vec; Tang LINE; Kipf GCN;
Hamilton GraphSAGE; Veličković GAT; Bordes TransE; Sun RotatE; Trouillon
ComplEx.

**Done when.** Node vs. edge vs. KG prediction tasks are distinguished.

# Part III — Practice

## Chapter 11 — Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Pitfalls
*File:* `chapters/11-evaluation-pitfalls.qmd`

**Purpose.** How to know whether an embedding is good — and the traps.

**Required sections**
1. Evaluating embeddings: linear probing, fine-tuning, k-NN, clustering,
   supervised heads.
2. Benchmarks: TAPE (proteins), BEND (DNA), scientific/omics benchmarks.
3. Data leakage: train/test homology, duplicate sequences, scaffold splits,
   time splits.
4. Distribution shift: new families, batch effects, organism transfer.
5. Metrics: AUROC/AUPRC, calibration, retrieval metrics, and their caveats.
6. Reproducibility and reporting checklist.

**Required artifacts.** Pitfall → detection → mitigation table; an evaluation
protocol decision flow.

**Key citations.** Rao TAPE; Dalla-Torre BEND; Whalen (homology leakage);
Bernett (leakage in bio); Luecken benchmarking; Chuang (splitting).

**Done when.** A reader can design a leak-free evaluation for a new embedding.

## Chapter 12 — Interpretability and Visualization
*File:* `chapters/12-interpretability-visualization.qmd`

**Purpose.** Making embeddings and their structure legible.

**Required sections**
1. Visualization: PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, PHATE — and the rules for honest use.
2. Neighborhood and local structure; trustworthiness/continuity metrics.
3. Probing: linear probes, structural probes, and what they can/can't show.
4. Attribution and attention: saliency, integrated gradients, attention caveats.
5. Latent-space arithmetic and directions (disentanglement).
6. Reporting checklist for embedding figures.

**Required artifacts.** Visualization-method comparison table; a "do/don't"
figure checklist.

**Key citations.** McInnes UMAP; Moon PHATE; Belinkov & Glass probing;
Jain/Rudin attention-is-not-explanation; Sundararajan integrated gradients.

**Done when.** The reader can produce an embedding figure that is not
misleading.

## Chapter 13 — Foundation Models and Emerging Directions
*File:* `chapters/13-foundation-models.qmd`

**Purpose.** The current frontier and open problems.

**Required sections**
1. What "foundation model" means in biology; scaling laws.
2. Modality-specific foundation models (recap and comparison).
3. Multimodal/generalist biological models and virtual cell efforts.
4. Agentic and reasoning systems over biological embeddings.
5. Open challenges: data curation, evaluation, compute, licensing, ethics.
6. Speculative outlook (clearly labelled as such).

**Required artifacts.** Foundation-model comparison matrix; a challenges table.

**Key citations.** Bommasani foundation models; Lin ESM-2; Dalla-Torre NT;
Bunne (toward a virtual cell); Cui scGPT; Boiko autonomous labs (with caveats).

**Done when.** Speculation is labelled and grounded where possible.

## Chapter 14 — Applications and Case Studies
*File:* `chapters/14-applications.qmd`

**Purpose.** End-to-end uses of embeddings.

**Required sections**
1. Variant effect prediction (protein and regulatory).
2. Drug discovery: property prediction, virtual screening, repurposing.
3. Annotation transfer and homology-free function prediction.
4. Antibody design and protein engineering (embedding-guided).
5. Clinical/biomarker embeddings and patient stratification.
6. A worked mini case study, reproducible in principle.

**Required artifacts.** Application → modality → method → metric table; a
pipeline diagram for the worked case study.

**Key citations.** Brandes (variant effects); Frazer (disease variant
prediction); Stokes (antibiotic discovery); Hie (antibody); Madani (protein
generation); Jumper AlphaFold2.

**Done when.** The worked case study states inputs, model, evaluation, and
limitations.

# Appendices

## Appendix A — Mathematical Background (`chapters/appendix-a-math.qmd`)
Linear algebra refresher, probability, information theory (entropy, KL,
mutual information), optimization basics. This is the canonical notation source.

## Appendix B — Tools and Datasets Cheat Sheet (`chapters/appendix-b-tools-data.qmd`)
Tables of major datasets (UniProt, PDB, Pfam, GTEx, GEO, Human Cell Atlas) and
libraries (PyTorch, Hugging Face, Biopython, RDKit, Scanpy, scvi-tools,
PyTorch Geometric, DGL), each with a one-line purpose and link.

## Appendix C — Glossary (`chapters/appendix-c-glossary.qmd`)
Alphabetical definitions of every bolded term used in the book.

## About `references.bib`
Single shared bibliography. Keys are `firstauthorYYYY` unless a well-known
acronym is clearer. Verifier checks: (a) key resolves in the text, (b) entry has
title + venue/year, (c) DOI or stable URL present for post-2000 work.
